This is expert testimony without a report. And to save time, no problem, but please I would ask for non-leading questions when eliciting expert information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, it even goes beyond expert opinion. You're asking for a judgement and whether my thoughts are mine or someone else's is not a question which can be put in general nor can it be answered in general terms. Please, next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In your brigade, when a document was being drafted and an operations officer from your staff was involved in it, was he working on your orders or under his own -- following his own idea of the document?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The operations officer has the duty and obligation to put everything that was decided upon by myself and my staff. He is not allowed to omit anything and needs to phrase the document precisely. That is why it is stated who drafted it, and for the most part it was the operations officer who did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we next have Prosecution document 65 ter number 5821. It is Directive 7/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where we find that it was drafted in the Main Staff of the VRS. You have had occasion to see this document as well in the course of your work.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The document, that is to say Directive 7/1, was drafted on the 31st of March, 1995. As we could see, Directive 7 was produced on the 8th of March, 1995. I'm interested in the following. Please bear with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm interested in page 5 in the B/C/S version and the same page in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We see here what tasks were issued to the Drina Corps in the document published by the Main Staff of the VRS. So as not to read all of it, please have a look at it and then I can ask a question, or perhaps everyone could check what I'm about to ask you. First of all, is it correct that in the tasks foreseen by -- [In English] I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where do you want to start reading, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Point 5.3.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah, Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that in the tasks foreseen by the Main Staff by virtue of this document pertaining to the Drina Corps, there are no tasks specifically designated as being aimed at the enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us briefly go back to Directive 7, that is to say the previous document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was Prosecution document 65 ter number 4001. In the English, it is easy. We need the last page. In the B/C/S we need page 21. I think that's what it was last time. Yes, the pages are correct in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In this directive by the Supreme Command in item 8 we find the following: "Send corps commander's decisions for approval to the commander of the VRS Main Staff seven days before carrying out the planned operation." In order to answer this question, we need to again see document which received the number P1465. It is the Drina Corps command order dated the 2nd of July. It is an order for active combat and the title is "Krivaja 95." Among the list of addressees, is there the Main Staff of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was sent to the brigade -- some brigades of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We see from the document that a task was ordered which had not been foreseen by Directive 7/1 and that the order was not sent to the Main Staff of the VRS in keeping of item 8 in Directive 7; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just, you know, Mr. President, the order of the -- the cover page order -- or letter from General Milovanovic is now put in the correct position, 65 ter 04001 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- for Directive 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At least that confusion has been removed. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm closing to the end so everybody knows. The next witness should be brought, although I don't know how long the re-direct will take.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you finish your cross-examination to start with.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In a couple of minute -- in a minute or two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, at least I'm bringing this to a close, so I just have a few more brief questions. As brigade commander you had a Chief of Staff, didn't you? At the same time was he your deputy well?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your absence, for example, if you were involved in Krivaja 95, is it correct that your Chief of Staff commanded your brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Part of the brigade. The larger part of the brigade in the defence zone, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Trivic, thank you for having answered our questions.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we ask whether the Prosecution has any need to re-examine the witness, Judge Fluegge has a question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: One or perhaps a couple of questions. Mr. Trivic, we dealt with Directive 7 and Directive 7/1. You told us that in July 1995 you haven't received Directive 7. Is my recollection correct, that you didn't receive it at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not receive it. At the time I did not receive these directives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Did you receive Directive 7/1 in July 1995 or between March and July 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think I did. That's what I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I put this question to you because you answered a question of Mr. Lukic in a different way, page 49, line 16. It was put to you by Mr. Lukic: "You have had occasion to see this document as well in the course of your work," whatever "in the course of your work" means. And then you answered: "Yes." How did you understand the question of Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood the question. I think it was quite correct but it also contained another part. "In your later work." So I think that is what is missing from this question, or rather, from the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Or rather, thank you for that clarification. If I understood you correctly, you were a colonel at that time in mid-1995 and the commander of the 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Who was your direct superior at that time, in July 1995? Who could issue orders to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The corps command issued orders to me, the commander of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Who was the direct superior to the commander of the Drina Corps at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The head of the Main Staff was his superior, if I understood your question correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, indeed that was my question. And that means it was the commander of the VRS; is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, no signing. I'll assist you in -- and no loud speaking, Mr. Mladic. Mr. Mladic, no loud speaking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, any questions in re-examination for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would like to clarify the last point. The Supreme Commander of the Republika Srpska was President Radovan Karadzic in July of 1995; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the commander of the VRS is General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As commander of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. I think that that would be the full title that he held.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you for clarifying that. I'll -- since we've been dealing with --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I just think that my friend misspoke. He should check. "As commander ..." Page 54, line 13: "The Supreme Commander of the Republika Srpska ..." I thought you meant "VRS."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. -- Colonel Trivic can sort that out for us, but I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I wondered whether there is any dispute about the positions of Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Mladic in this respect. If there is not, then I consider just an introduction to questions that may follow. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: These words from Directive 7 directed to the Drina Corps to make life unbearable for the Muslim population. You told us you didn't get Directive 7, but did you get those words in another document directed to you?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you to remind me if you have such a document, that is. After all these years whether something like that did arrive or did not arrive, I don't want to speculate. During the conversations I had with you, during the proofing, and if you have an answer that I provided, please do remind me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't remember. But these are amazing words. I won't repeat them again. "Make life unbearable for the people." Certainly you would have remembered those words if they had been given to you from your superiors. Yes or no: Do you remember or not?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume I would remember. These are very grave words. But let's not go into any further explanations. I assume that if they had been put that way I would have remembered. But here in this context of this directive, they do not have that meaning. I explained -- I tried to explain, present -- well, not explain, sorry, I meant I tried to present my point of view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You're supposed to present facts you have observed. The answer is simply, therefore, that the witness says that he doesn't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we go to 65 ter 04190.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Colonel, take your -- take your time with this. We see that it's from the commander of the Drina Corps in March 1995 -- sorry, March 20th, 1995. And it's to the command of all the brigades, including yours, 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade, order for Defence and combat operations, operative number 7, and then it talks about the enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to page 6 in the English and page 3 in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's look in that first B/C/S paragraph in the Cyrillic and -- sorry, under paragraph 2, the first paragraph under paragraph 2 in the Cyrillic. It's the top of the page, the fourth line down in the English. "By planned and well-thought-out combat operations create an unbearable situation of total insecurity with no hope of further survival or life for the inhabitants of Srebrenica and Zepa." In your own words, those grave words were directed to you. Do you now recall them?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that we discussed this in some situation but this is the 23rd.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Colonel, do you now remember receiving these words in this document? Simple question, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. No, I do not remember because they were not addressed to me because I do not have positions vis-a-vis Srebrenica and Zepa. Quite simply, these were not my tasks. I did not register them or did I have any need to register them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Colonel, are you saying when you get an order from your commander that you don't read the complete order so that you don't know what your neighbours are up to around you? And remember your testimony regarding the Krivaja 95 Operation.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think I'm being superficial and that I hadn't read this. I just say that it wasn't my task and that I don't remember. As for these words, on the 20th of March, this did not pertain to my unit at all. I did not have positions vis-a-vis Srebrenica and Zepa and that is why I attached less importance to this part of this order for active combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer this document into evidence, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P1468, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I would also offer Directive 7 at this time, which is 04001.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar -- Mr. Lukic, I take it that there is no objection? Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P1469, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1469 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Directive 7/1, 05821.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P1470, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Colonel, going back to the Bratunac Brigade headquarters, the situation as you've described, you spoke briefly on this topic. Were orders given at that meeting to have troops secure the road Bratunac-Konjevic Polje-Milici as the bulk of the forces were going to Zepa?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Tasks were issued to tasks -- to units that cover areas of their defence; that is to say, to secure roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm speaking specifically of the Bratunac-Konjevic Polje-Milici road.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was referred to, that these units should secure that road if the road goes through their areas of defence and also that reinforcements from the police should be sought.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when you say "police," do you mean the MUP, the Ministry of the Interior police?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who -- who issued those orders at the meeting that night?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was discussed. No order was issued. I think that General Krstic gave a task to the commanders who were affected that evening, but there was no specifically written order also in terms of asking the MUP, the police, in that area for their assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, and I'm not asking, as you know, when I say "orders" or "tasks," I'm not -- we know many of these aren't written at this point. In the past you weren't sure if it was General Krstic or General Mladic that issued those tasks to the brigades. Could it have been General Mladic that issued the order or the task?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think -- or rather, it's not that I think. Krstic was the one who issued orders. General Mladic, in my view -- actually, the only order that was issued by General Mladic to General Krstic was to prepare for Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the 13th very briefly. You have referred to the packed football field of prisoners as disarmed -- what was the term you used?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Disarmed enemy forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. And I don't want to get into this in detail, but I do have one question. You've cited General Eisenhower as your source for that regarding the German prisoners after the war in 1945. Did you cite that knowing the many, many thousands of German prisoners that perished in the custody of the Allies under that designation?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just used the term that General Eisenhower had used according to literature. He avoided the qualification of German soldiers as prisoners of war for certain reasons. He defined them, qualified them, as disarmed enemy forces. When they later became -- I mean, their status when they were being disarmed was -- he qualified them as disarmed enemy forces. When did they become prisoners of war? Probably later when they were recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It was a simple question. Did you know that many thousands of German prisoners had perished when you cited that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely, the literature that describes these events mentions the reasons why the commander of the Allied Forces qualified these forces as disarmed enemy forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. We can go to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Why not --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- another subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Why not answer the question? Is there anything that keeps you off from doing that? I establish that you're doing it. Mr. McCloskey, next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to your diary, something that we're familiar with, because we got into Zepa a bit and so I want to ask you about a couple of things related to Zepa and the status of civilians or -- or prisoners, which was related to the Kasaba folks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So if we could go back to what is now P1467. It's MFI'd. And it should be page 73 in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we'll wait for your -- there's your diary. And we see that's number 1 -- you've numbered it 1 in red and we see the number 1 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to the next -- it's actually page 71 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But it's your number 2. Sorry, it's number 72 in e-court and your number 2. And we see here something entitled: "Major-General Krstic," and then there is four points. And I want to start with point 2: "The brilliant victory in Srebrenica is the biggest boost to morale." So is -- what's General Krstic -- what's this reflect, these notes? Is it like a talk from General Krstic, something like that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is an introduction at this gathering, that was this meeting, with subordinates and that's how the meeting started. Primarily in terms of what he had to say to us before we started reporting and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And could you read number 3 for us, slowly.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. "The situation in the Srebrenica enclave and Birac." And then the next bullet point: "Small groups of civilians." Next one: "Small armed groups." And --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's okay. I don't want to get into the brigades. So we see here General Krstic on the 16th of July when speaking of the groups of Muslims still in the area, he's able to distinguish groups of civilians and armed groups clearly, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how I recorded what he said, succinctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go up to number 1: "The VRS VK has decided that eastern parts of RS must be liberated from the Turks." He actually said that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that those buses we saw on the 26th of July, those were the civilians from Zepa being shipped out. So by the end of July there were no more civilians or people of any number either in the Srebrenica enclave or the Zepa enclave, were there?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm a soldier. Allow me. I've already answered several times, either to your questions or questions put by your associates, that this term, "Turks," "Chetniks," "balijas," whatever else pertains to soldiers. That's what we called each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's keep going. Let's go to page 70 in your diary. It's just a couple of more pages away. And at this period of time you're in combat with the forces of the Zepa Brigade, right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Could we -- well, I think that is it. Can you let me see the date?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This was three pages on from your date of 16 July with no dates in between. Okay. Tell us what this means: "PAD for "launching aerial bombs to come tomorrow to Gusinac "Mitar Komljenovic "to report to Rogatica at 0800 hours." What's a PAD and what are for launching aerial bombs? What's that stuff?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a motor vehicle with a makeshift pad attached to the chassis from which, with the assistance of the pads, one can launch an aerial bomb to an area. One can launch an aerial bomb to an area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So this pad is on the back of a truck; right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is well lit to the chassis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that acts as sort of a ramp by which you shoot this bomb off with rockets?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one needs an explosive charge, something that will make it fly. It ejects it from the ramp, and depending on the angle of the launcher, that aerial bomb can reach a certain distance. The bigger the angle, especially over 45 degrees, the trajectory is shorter. If you put it under 45 degrees the trajectory is longer. However, it is an improvised launcher that we refer to as a ramp which enabled the firing or launching of an aerial bomb. There were such aerial bombs in certain warehouses where they had not been withdrawn. I think I explained this already and it can be found in the transcript of my previous testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when you say "aerial bombs," you mean bombs designed to be dropped from airplanes?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a jacket of such an aerial bomb. The casings belonged to aerial bombs but there were different explosive charges. For the most part such a device has a psychological impact because it is a large calibre and detonates in a certain area. Originally they are designed to be dropped from airplanes, but on this occasion they were not dropped from planes, they were launched from these improvised launching pads or ramps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But just for the psychological impact?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for the most part. They were called SOWs [phoen]. They did not have a significant effect other than making a loud noise, having a psychological impact on any fighters in the area. It doesn't mean, though, that parts of such a jacket cannot injure someone close by. There can be consequences like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And in Zepa there were villages and civilian populations all interspersed around much of the army, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At certain distances away from each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How many of these devices did you hear go off in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This piece of information that I noted does not say it was used but that it was supposed to arrive. I think - and I'm almost certain - that none were used. There was only one such ramp on one vehicle in that area, generally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That you knew of. Okay. You also talked about the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, "that you knew of" is comment. If you have questions for the witness, put them to the witness, but do not complete the answers of the witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You, in your cross-examination, talked about an agreement with the various sides, the Muslim side, the Serbian side, and their evacuation. Would it have been proper under your training as a JNA officer in meeting with the opposing side to tell them, "Civilians of Zepa, you need to leave. And if you don't leave, we will begin a military attack." Is that proper?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is this leading?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's just a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The issue was whether it was a leading question or not and whether you think that you could lead in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't think it suggests an answer. It's just a question whether that's fair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you aware that this was the strategy employed by General Tolimir in dealing with the Muslim population in his meeting with -- with their representatives?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we go to 65 ter 4175.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we're waiting for it, Mr. McCloskey, I take it that we agree on the following: That a leading question is a question which either suggests an answer or includes assumed facts which have not yet been established. And I think it's rather the latter of the two which was making Mr. Lukic rising to his feet. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry this is hard to read. If we could blow it up for you so you can get a read on it. We see it's 13 July and we now know that's the -- the day that you went to the Zepa operation. It's from the command of the 1st Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade, which is Rogatica. And it -- the last page is under the name of General Zdravko Tolimir. And we see the -- the first -- the first page, and let's see who it's to: The Main Staff of the VRS, service for intelligence -- or, sorry, sector for intelligence and security; the command of the Drina Corps, department for intelligence and security; and for General Krstic, your commander of this operation. And let's go -- we see that it starts out with: On 13 July there was a meeting between Hamdija Torlak, president of the Zepa Executive Committee, Mujo Omanovic -- and I won't read the rest of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And let's now look at paragraph -- it's 5, which is on that front page. It's a little hard to read. Page 2 in the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And here General Tolimir says: "We rejected their first request and we made a condition that all necessary consultations had to be completed by 1500 hours and that the evacuation had to start at that time. We have conditioned this within an alternative solution - military force. We guarantee the evacuation of all civilian population and military aged men who surrender their weapons, as well as the safety for the civilians who decide to stay and accept RS authority." So on the evening of 13 July, you're gearing up for the Zepa operation. Did General Krstic inform you that there had been this ultimatum to the representatives regarding the upcoming operation?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer this document into evidence, 4175.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P1471, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: One last document and then just a couple of questions related to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How much time would you still need? Should we take a break first? I suggest that we -- we are now at a little bit over one hour. If you finish within next three or four minutes, would you have further questions then? Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Two by now, one rising from your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. How much time would you need, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just a few minutes. I want to show him one other document and ask him if he heard about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then also looking at Mr. Lukic, because if we would finish before and then take a break, then for the next witness we could prepare necessary measures. But that would go some ten minutes then beyond what is the usual time. Then it's appreciated that Mr. Mladic assists. Please proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me show you another document from General Tolimir and ask you if you'd seen it on the topic of how civilians were treated and the intentions of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And as we'll see, this is dated 21 July 1995, again from the command of the Rogatica Brigade. And it's to the VRS Main Staff, to General Miletic personally. Let me see if I can clear something up. General Miletic at the time, was his position the chief of operations and training for the Main Staff or just chief of operations? If you know.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I recall, the position was the chief of operations and training or something of the sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you know a Colonel Obradovic who was the actual chief of operations at the time at the Main Staff, under Miletic?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I met him in that organ. They had a part in charge of training and education and another part for operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let me ask you if you've heard of paragraph 4: "We believe that it is more profitable to hold direct negotiations after inflicting losses on the enemy's manpower. We ask you to provide us with means to destroy the enemy defence in the area of Brezova Ravan and Purtici." Okay. I'm not in my questions suggesting any difficulties with that. But then: "It would be most profitable to destroy them by using chemical means or aerosol mines and bombs. By using these means, we would cause the fall of Zepa and surrender of the Muslims. We will continue with combat operations with direct attack weapons to break through in the mentioned directions." Now we hear this -- were you aware of a proposal to use chemical means in the Zepa operation? And let me be specific: It is the Prosecution position we are talking about tear-gas chemicals, unless you know of any other.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't aware of this plan or activity. Given the area, I don't think such means would be used because we were in close contact. The area of the Zepa valley is configured in such a way that both sides will sustain casualties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you've answered the question by saying that you weren't aware. Please proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So would you be surprised if I showed you the documents that showed chemical tear-gas, rocket-propelled grenades, and hand-grenades?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, whether the witness -- if he says he is not aware of it, he's not here to learn the history unless you want to suggest to him that he did not answer in accordance with the truth. But he's not here to be taught; he's here to give evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm just trying to save a little time, Mr. President, because I have those documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm just telling him and seeing if that will help refresh his recollection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, okay. Is there any chance that you -- if you look at documents that you might remember, or are you certain that you never heard of the use of tear-gas in the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In response to one of your previous questions today, I said that I don't recall ever having stated that I was aware that chemical weapons were used.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness repeat the very end of his answer because he trailed off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you repeat the last part of your answer. I -- perhaps I can already say that it was not suggested to you that you said so - at least, Mr. McCloskey, that's how I understood it - but that Mr. McCloskey says that documents would indicate that tear-gas would have been used and whether looking at those documents, whether that might refresh your recollection in this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Almost, Mr. President. Tear-gas supplies were delivered to the forward command post. I don't use --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, I said -- therefore, I didn't say "prove" -- well, in any case, you say "use." Well, any document that would establish that tear-gas was delivered, is there any chance that that might refresh your recollection?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, no. I had no such information and I don't recall that there was any reference to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the last paragraph beginning with: "We believe ..." Were you aware of that proposal being made?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please repeat your question because I didn't understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you aware that this last proposal, that this statement in the last paragraph was made? Did you ever hear about this?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer 5370 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P1472, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections, therefore admitted. Mr. Lukic. Was that your last question, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If we can briefly go to page 60, line 13, of today's transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Today Judge Orie stated that you did not answer his question and that you did not wish to. Did you at any point refuse to answer Judge Orie's questions? Do you remember it having been said today?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember it. Based on my -- yesterday's experience, I am not even prepared to discuss this, taking into consideration the position of the Judges and my role in the courtroom. But I do recall that he said so concerning those who perished after being captured; that is to say, the German disarmed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know, then, that many thousands of German prisoners perished after the operation of capturing them, and did you connect the use of the term you used with that situation?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. I simply referred to the way the Allied Forces commander avoided having termed those disarmed enemy forces as POWs. I did not analyse it in any expert sense. I simply stated the fact that he did so. The sources that refer to his position also describe that people did perish; however, I cannot say anything specifically. That is why I did not answer directly to Mr. McCloskey. I did not research it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I always prefer to be quoted correctly. I established that the witness did not answer the question. I didn't say anything about whether he wished to do or not. He didn't do it. I establish that you are doing it, is what I said. Before I said: "Is there anything that keeps you off from doing that?" And that was answering the question. I did not express myself in terms of refusal or wishes, just I established that the witness did not answer the question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Actually, I don't have any other questions. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then, Mr. Trivic, this concludes your testimony in this Court. I would like to thank you very much for coming a long way to The Hague and for having answered the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench. May I invite you to follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before the witness leaves, can I get the permission to see the witness now after he leaves for one minute?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course. I take it that if -- the Defence is free to speak with the witness unless you have any other plans of re-calling, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No. Of course, the witness people will have him --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- and will take Mr. Lukic over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There is only one practical matter and I would like to move into private session for a second.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. We'll take a break and we'll resume at ten minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good afternoon, Witness. I am not going to use your name because protective measures apply for your testimony. I therefore will call you Witness RM306. Witness, before you give evidence, the rules require that you make a solemn declaration. The text is now handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness RM306, I first would like to inform you that the request for an extension of protective measures has been granted. That means that the outside world will not see your face, they will not hear your own voice, and we'll address you not by your own name but as Witness RM306. Before we proceed, I'd like to address the following matter: We cannot exclude that you in answering truthfully the questions that you would have to make a statement which might to incriminate yourself. Now, a witness, you are a witness, may object -- yes, there seems to be a -- one second, please. Now, a witness - and you are a witness - may object to making any statement which might tend to incriminate yourself, and then, of course, the Chamber will then consider whether you nevertheless have to answer that question. But just to inform you that if you feel that a truthful answer might incriminate yourself, you may object to answer that question. Is that clear to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Ms. Lee, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: RM306
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: The Court has ordered certain protective measures with respect to you and your evidence here today. These include the use of a pseudonym, distortion of your image and voice, and now I would -- so I would not refer you by your name, but I'll refer you as witness or RM306.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: May I please have 65 ter number 28906 which is under seal pulled up in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Witness, please take a look at the document on the screen before you. Is that your name and date of birth?

utterances.speaker: RM306
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution tenders 65 ter 28906 into evidence under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P1473, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted under seal. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: May I please have 65 ter number 28905 brought into e-court under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: And while it's being brought up: Witness, is it correct that you provided a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal in October of 2000 in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: RM306
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: And have you previously appeared before this Tribunal in three cases; namely in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, one second. Apparently there is some problem with the audio for Mr. Mladic. May it -- could it be caused by using the -- not the exact socket due to the voice distortion? Witness, could you please speak a few words because most important is that Mr. Mladic is able to hear the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Can we move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And it lists three full days. So I'm presuming that he reviewed the entirety of that testimony, whereas the proffered Rule 92 ter transcript is a selection. Therefore, if he says the entirety of my testimony is accurate, including any corrections you might have made that the Prosecution has not included in their 92 ter transcript is not the same thing as authenticating this selection, this extract.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, if you have attested to the whole of it, would that in any way affect that part of it, would be covered by that?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It may, Your Honour. Part of it may not be accurate because he believes it's been corrected in the part that is not listed. He doesn't know what's been selected by the Prosecution, just like my client doesn't know because they listened to the audiotape as a whole.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but if I say that the totality of the evidence is accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If now a portion of that evidence is tendered, would that then not be part of what the witness attested to as being accurate?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The totality would be, including totality meaning everything he said afterwards that may affect what he said in these selections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But is there any correction which you consider relevant in this context to which you would like to draw the attention? Because I do understand that if in the non-selected portion there would be a correction to anything, that we would miss that then.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, is there any such thing you noticed in the totality, because I take it you have gone through the totality of the evidence? Are there any?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I will be raising them in my cross-examination, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There are?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then we'll have it marked for identification for the time being, and then we'll hear during cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since you have identified such portions, we'll MFI it first. Mr. Registrar, the document would receive number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 128905 receives P1474.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is marked for identification and under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Further, I urge the parties - and I did make a mistake myself in that respect as well - not to refer to the previous case by name. That is one. Second, Mr. Ivetic, any objections against the associated exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: None, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, then for the associated exhibits?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 04824 receives P1475 and 65 ter 14173 receives P1476, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1475 and P1476 are admitted into evidence. Ms. Lee, no need to have them under seal?

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I would suggest that we continue for five more minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Perhaps I could -- perhaps this is a good time to read a brief summary of the witness's evidence. Can we please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the reason why I wanted to continue for five minutes, Ms. Lee, is in order to make the witness feel perhaps a bit more comfortable because until now it was only procedural matters. I suggest that you read the summary tomorrow and that you put your first questions to the witness and then we'll adjourn.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, except that my first question will lead to a topic that will take more than five minutes, and I was just wondering if I -- if it would be best to ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Under those circumstances, we'll adjourn earlier. Witness, the reason why I suggested that we would continue for another five minutes is because you have been exposed, until now, mainly to procedural matters, whereas no question has yet been put to you. Now we'll start with your real testimony tomorrow. We'd like to see you back tomorrow morning, and meanwhile I have to instruct you that you should not speak or communicate in whatever way about the testimony you are about to give. Is that clear to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will then adjourn for the day after we've moved into closed session, and we will resume tomorrow, Thursday, the 23rd of May, at 9.30 in the morning in this same courtroom III. We move into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 23rd day of May, 2013, at 9.30 a.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.17 p.m.,
